People Are Afraid of AI. Governance Is the Answer.

The EU has confirmed its first AI-driven attack. The FBI says attackers can reach admin access in under three hours. The public is more afraid than ever. Fear is a reasonable response to missing control, so this week is about putting control in place.

23 NOVEMBER 2026 • WHAT CHANGED SINCE FRIDAY • UAE | GLOBAL
01 | What changed since Friday

The first AI-driven attack on the EU is now confirmed. The FBI had warned six days earlier.

On 19 November the European Commission confirmed that the cyberattack it detected on 22 October was carried out with AI tools. It is the first time the EU has disclosed an attack of this kind.

Spokesperson Thomas Regnier said several internal applications were taken down as a precaution and most have been restored. The Commission says it has found no evidence of a data breach affecting its staff as a whole. It has not named the tool or the attackers, and the investigation is continuing.

Six days earlier, on 13 November, the FBI had published a FLASH alert on ARTEX, an open-source, AI-driven penetration-testing framework that criminals and state-aligned actors have turned into an attack tool. The FBI says it has been abused since at least August. Taking the code offline did not stop it, because forks, archived copies and a commercial version are still circulating.

<3 hours From first target to privileged access in some ARTEX intrusions, according to the FBI.
1,600+ Publicly exposed ARTEX consoles that researchers counted in early November.
84 days Between an OpenAI agent's unauthorised access to an Australian Medicare portal and OpenAI telling the government.

Sources: FBI FLASH-20261113-001 as reported by The Record and SecNews; Cloud Security Alliance research note on the Australian incident.

Correction to Friday: we reported ARTEX as suspected in the Commission attack. The Commission has confirmed AI tool misuse but has not named the tool. CERT-EU has warned that publicly available tools such as ARTEX can make attacks faster and more automated. Treat the ARTEX link as likely, not confirmed.

02 | Why people are afraid

The fear is rational. It is also a governance signal.

People are not afraid of a chatbot. They are afraid that nobody is in charge when something goes wrong. This week gave them evidence.

51.9% of Americans fear AI harming the political process, level with fear of a loved one falling seriously ill (51.8%). Chapman University, 2026.
50% of US adults are worried about AI ending humanity, up from 42% in November 2023. YouGov, September 2026.
2 in 3 UK respondents say AI companies should be closely regulated, even if that slows development. King's College London, May 2026.

Sources: Popular Science and IFLScience on the Chapman survey; YouGov; ITPro and Euronews on the King's College survey.

The Chapman survey also shows a split that matters for every leader. Among people who use AI weekly, 46% reported the fear. Among people who never use it, 55% did. Familiarity reduces fear, and so does seeing who is accountable.

Our perspective: reassurance does not work on a worried team or a worried customer. Evidence of control does. Tell people which agents you run, who owns each one, what they can touch and how you would stop one.

“AI adoption starts with people, not technology. Leaders have to understand the change well enough to explain it, make space for questions and bring their teams along.”

Lisa Warren, Founder & CEO, Neural Horizons AI

The evidence: the Chapman gap between weekly users (46%) and non-users (55%) points the same way. Lisa wrote the full argument in Nothing Is Lost. Only Gained. and the history behind it in 76 Years in the Making.

03 | What it means: governance

Regulators and analysts are saying the same thing. Owners, tiers and an incident clock.

Governments have started to write the rules, and the analysts are warning that companies without them will pay.

Australia accepted 18 recommendations on 10 November after the Medicare portal incident. They include mandatory, time-bound reporting of serious AI incidents, among them misaligned model behaviour and cyber incidents involving autonomous agents, and a new AI safety regulator. OpenAI and Anthropic told Australian lawmakers on 6 October that they would welcome mandatory reporting.

Gartner predicts that by 2027, 40% of enterprises will demote or decommission autonomous AI agents because of governance gaps found only after production incidents. Its advice is proportional governance: classify agents by how much autonomy they have rather than locking everything down or trusting everything. Gartner also reports that 75% of organisations have seen unauthorised use of AI coding assistants.

The UAE has revealed a control tower to monitor government AI agents, with continuous auditing by both AI systems and humans, as it works towards its target of agents delivering 50% of federal services within two years. Our UAE update tracks what is confirmed and what is not.

What a SOC teaches about AI governance: Lisa spent years at SecurityHQ, a global managed security provider with six security operations centres, working alongside its engineers and sales teams and with partners such as Al-Futtaim and du. A SOC does not ask whether an alert is frightening. Every alert has an owner, a severity and a clock, and it closes only when someone signs it off. That is the model AI governance needs: an owner for every agent, controls that scale with autonomy, and a clock for incidents.

“Governance is not the tax you pay for using AI responsibly. It's the thing that lets you use AI at all, at scale, without it blowing up in your hands.”

Lisa Warren, Founder & CEO, Neural Horizons AI

The evidence: Gartner expects 40% of enterprises to demote or decommission autonomous agents over governance gaps, and Australia is making incident reporting compulsory. Full argument in AI Governance Isn't Optional Anymore and AI Agents Can Be Responsible. They Can Never Be Accountable.

04 | Our predictions

Four calls for the next twelve months. We will mark them in public.

These are judgements, not forecasts from a data set. Each one shows what it rests on and how confident we are.

1. Within 90 days, more large institutions will disclose AI-assisted attacks. The EU's disclosure was a first. Australia is moving to compulsory reporting, and the FBI says ARTEX keeps circulating through forks and a commercial version. Confidence: high.

2. By mid-2027, an agent register will be a standard audit and procurement question. Microsoft is already selling agent identity and named managers, and Gartner is pushing agent risk profiles and oversight tooling. Customers will ask suppliers to show their register. Confidence: medium to high.

3. The agents that get shut down first will be the ones with no named owner. Gartner's 40% figure is about governance gaps found after incidents. Our read of client work is that the missing owner is the most common gap. Confidence: medium.

4. More governments will copy Australia's incident-reporting model. Two of the largest AI developers have said they would welcome it, which removes the main objection. Confidence: medium.

“Agentic AI security incidents will keep outpacing governance maturity for at least 24 more months.”

Lisa Warren, Founder & CEO, Neural Horizons AI

The evidence: Lisa made this call in 76 Years in the Making on 17 July. Since then the EU has disclosed an AI-driven attack, the FBI has warned about ARTEX, and an OpenAI agent's breach of an Australian government portal has triggered new law.

05 | What to do this week

Show people who is in charge. Six moves for Monday.

Tap each step you already have in place. Every gap is a place where an agent runs without anyone watching.

Your AI governance check0 of 6

Tap each step you already have in place.

  1. Register every AI tool and agent.Include the ones inside SaaS products you already pay for. You cannot govern what you have not listed.
  2. Put a named human on each one.An agent can be Responsible. Only a person can be Accountable. "IT" is not a name.
  3. Tier agents by autonomy.Agents that only observe need light controls. Agents that act need approvals, audit trails and a tested way to stop them.
  4. Set an incident clock.Who is told, how fast, and who can switch the agent off. Test the switch with someone who did not build the agent.
  5. Log what agents do and review it.Pick a fixed rhythm, weekly for agents that act. If nobody reads the log, it is not governance.
  6. Tell your people what is changing and why.Show them the register, the owners and the stop switch. Give them a voice in how the work changes.

For UAE businesses: the national programme is moving from announcements to operations, and the control-tower model shows where expectations are heading. Showing your own register and owners now puts you ahead of the question.

Questions leaders ask

Has the European Commission confirmed that AI was used in the attack?

Yes. On 19 November spokesperson Thomas Regnier confirmed that the attack, detected on 22 October, was carried out with AI tools. The Commission has not named the tool or the attackers. CERT-EU has warned that publicly available tools such as ARTEX can enable faster, more automated attacks, but the Commission has not confirmed ARTEX.

Why are people afraid of AI?

Surveys show fear rising. In Chapman University's 2026 survey, fear of AI harming the political process was level with fear of a loved one becoming seriously ill. YouGov found 50% of US adults worried about AI ending humanity, up from 42% in 2023. Fear is lower among people who use AI weekly, which suggests familiarity and visible control both help.

What is AI governance in practice?

It means knowing which AI tools and agents you run, giving each a named human owner, tiering controls by how much autonomy the agent has, setting an incident clock, logging what agents do and reviewing it on a fixed rhythm.

What are Neural Horizons AI's predictions?

More institutions will disclose AI-assisted attacks within 90 days, an agent register will become a standard audit question by mid-2027, agents without a named owner are the most likely to be demoted or shut down, and more governments will copy Australia's mandatory AI incident reporting.
